Baby & Child

Poland syndrome: variable features, diagnosis and individual care

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Poland syndrome is a rare condition present from birth in which a chest muscle is underdeveloped or absent, usually on one side. Other features vary widely: some people have hand or rib differences, while others have few visible changes. Care should be based on function, health and the person’s own priorities, rather than an assumption that every difference needs surgery.

The defining chest-muscle difference

The main feature is underdevelopment or absence of part of the pectoralis major, especially its sternocostal portion attached toward the breastbone and ribs. This large, fan-shaped muscle helps move the upper arm. The smaller pectoralis minor lies underneath and helps move the shoulder blade; it may also differ, but its absence is not required in every case.

Chest shape may look flatter or hollow on the affected side. Nearby muscles, including the latissimus dorsi in the back or the serratus anterior along the chest wall, can also be underdeveloped in some people. The particular muscles and tissues involved matter more than assuming that everyone has the same pattern.

Breast, nipple, skin and rib features

There may be less breast tissue, a smaller or absent nipple or areola, reduced tissue under the skin, or less or differently placed underarm hair on the affected side. Breast asymmetry can become more apparent during puberty. These features do not determine a person’s worth or make treatment for appearance obligatory.

Some people have shortened or missing ribs or rib cartilage, or another chest-wall shape difference. Many have little effect on day-to-day health, while more extensive chest-wall changes can affect breathing or require specialist assessment. A rib difference is not present in everyone, and a photograph cannot determine its extent.

Shoulder, arm and hand differences

A high or underdeveloped shoulder blade, sometimes called Sprengel deformity, can affect shoulder movement or create a raised outline near the base of the neck. The arm or forearm may be shorter, including differences in the radius and ulna. The team assesses motion and useful activities rather than appearance alone.

The hand on the same side may have short, small or missing finger bones and joined fingers. Brachydactyly means short fingers, syndactyly means joined fingers, and symbrachydactyly describes a combination of underdevelopment, often with short or joined fingers. Central fingers such as the index and middle may be involved; thumb features and severity vary. Hand involvement is not mandatory for Poland syndrome.

How much can the features vary?

Someone may have only a chest-muscle difference with a functional hand, while another has more complex chest and upper-limb differences. Even relatives with a similar diagnosis may have different features. It is congenital, but mild cases may not be recognized until adolescence or adulthood, especially when breast or chest asymmetry becomes clearer.

Rare internal-organ differences have been reported, including kidney, lung or heart-position changes. The specialist decides what assessment is needed rather than assuming all are present. Differences on both sides are unusual and need careful review for other diagnoses; published bilateral reports do not prove that every symmetrical chest difference is Poland syndrome.

What is known about the cause?

The exact cause is uncertain. One leading hypothesis is a disturbance in blood supply to the developing chest and upper limb early in pregnancy, involving vessels related to the subclavian artery around the sixth week. The site and extent of a disturbance might help explain variable features, but this is a proposed mechanism, not a proven event in every individual.

You may see the term Poland sequence: a sequence describes a pattern that may follow an initial developmental disturbance. Related vascular-development hypotheses have been discussed for conditions such as Möbius and Klippel–Feil syndromes and Sprengel differences; these are not interchangeable diagnoses or conditions everyone with Poland syndrome will develop. Families should not be told that a particular ordinary parental action has been proved to cause it.

Family history and how common it is

Most cases occur without another known affected relative. Rare families have more than one affected person, sometimes with subtle features in a parent or sibling. Genetic counseling can discuss the family pattern, whether examination of relatives is useful and whether testing for another or overlapping condition is indicated. There is no single universal test that confirms or excludes every clinical case.

The syndrome is named after Alfred Poland’s nineteenth-century description. Reported frequency varies and mild cases may be missed, so a precise population number is uncertain. Reports generally find more males and more right-sided cases, but these trends do not exclude females or left-sided cases and are not a prediction of severity. A family’s recurrence advice should be individualized rather than based on a fixed percentage from an article.

How is it diagnosed?

Diagnosis usually begins with a clinical examination and history. The clinician looks at the chest muscles, breast and nipple area, ribs, shoulder, arm and hand, and assesses function. Similar asymmetry can have other causes, so a hand difference or uneven chest alone is not enough for self-diagnosis. Obvious cases may be recognized at birth; others are identified later.

Ultrasound is often the first imaging method to clarify muscle and soft-tissue differences without radiation. X-rays may help evaluate bones when indicated. The team may also assess the heart, kidneys or other structures according to the clinical pattern. CT or MRI is selected for a specific question, an inconclusive examination or surgical planning; CT is not a routine first test for every child, and radiation or possible sedation must be considered.

A care plan that fits the person

Care may involve a pediatrician, genetics service, hand or orthopedic team, chest-wall and reconstructive specialists, physiotherapy or occupational therapy and psychological support. Not everyone needs every specialist or an operation. Priorities include breathing where relevant, comfortable movement, useful hand function, daily activities and the person’s goals.

Follow-up can review growth, changing movement, chest or breast development and any symptoms. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy may help with range of motion, strength, adaptations and activities, but cannot promise to regrow an absent muscle. Exercises and any splints should be selected for the individual; do not force joints or copy an aggressive routine from an image or online advice.

When hand or chest surgery is considered

Hand surgery may be discussed for joined fingers or other differences when it could improve useful function or growth. The type and timing depend on the anatomy, development and goals; there is no single operation or age for all children. Ask about likely benefit, alternatives, scars, stiffness, possible further procedures and rehabilitation.

For selected people, chest-wall or breast reconstruction may involve fat grafting, an implant, tissue transfer or structural rib work. These are different options for different problems, not a package everyone needs. Growth, available tissue, physical and psychological readiness and the person’s wishes influence planning. Surgery has risks and may need revision; it does not guarantee perfect symmetry, normal strength or a one-time permanent result.

Support, outlook and safety

Many people have mild features and good everyday function; others need more complex care. No single photograph, population ratio or surgical case series predicts an individual’s outcome. Listen to the child or adult’s preferences, protect privacy, address bullying and offer support for body image or relationships without making surgery the condition for confidence or acceptance.

Arrange review for new pain, reduced movement, activity-related breathing difficulty or concerns about growth or a postoperative wound. Follow the treating team’s wound and rehabilitation instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips or skin, sudden confusion, or a child who is limp or not responding normally needs immediate emergency care; do not assume a new acute symptom is just the congenital chest difference.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The 2020 expert consensus identifies pectoralis major involvement as the defining feature and supports clinical diagnosis, ultrasound-first clarification and selective further imaging. Its recommendations combine published evidence and expert experience, reflecting the limits of research in this rare condition.

MedlinePlus Genetics describes variable features, possible later recognition and uncertain causes and inheritance. A 2025 pediatric reconstruction study involves a selected surgical group, not all people with Poland syndrome; it supports attention to development, expectations, risks and psychosocial needs rather than universal outcome promises.

Currently available pediatric hand and chest services describe individual assessment and options. NHS emergency breathing advice supports urgent escalation for acute severe symptoms. Older source publication dates are retained; these are not described as new 2026 syndrome guidelines.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize growth and symptom notes, appointment questions and care plans. It cannot diagnose Poland syndrome from an image, select surgery or exercises, predict recurrence or replace specialist and emergency care.

When to seek help

Do not force a child’s joints, start unsupervised corrective exercises or assume surgery is required. Use individualized postoperative and rehabilitation instructions. Severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips or skin, sudden confusion, or a limp or unresponsive child needs immediate emergency care. New pain, reduced movement, breathing changes or wound concerns need assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Poland syndrome mainly involves an underdeveloped or absent part of pectoralis major; other muscles and hand features vary.
  • A person can have Poland syndrome without joined or short fingers, and mild cases may be recognized later.
  • The cause is uncertain; vascular-development explanations are hypotheses and most cases have no known family history.
  • Clinical assessment and selected imaging guide care; routine CT or surgery is not required for everyone.
  • Treatment and support should respect function, development and personal wishes, with realistic benefits and risks.

Frequently asked questions

What features can Poland syndrome include?

A chest-muscle difference, usually on one side, is central. Breast, nipple, skin, ribs, shoulder, arm or hand may also differ, but the pattern varies. Short or joined fingers are possible, not required in every case.

What causes it?

The exact cause remains uncertain. An early developmental blood-supply disturbance is a leading hypothesis, not proof of what happened in each person. Most cases occur without family history; rare familial patterns warrant individualized genetic counseling.

How is it diagnosed?

A clinician assesses the chest and related features and function, sometimes supported by ultrasound or other selected tests. Diagnosis is not always made at birth. CT is not a routine first test for all children; similar findings can have other causes.

How is it treated?

Treatment depends on symptoms, function, growth and personal priorities. Observation, therapy or adaptations may be appropriate. Selected hand, chest-wall or breast surgery can be discussed with specialists, but is not mandatory and benefits and complications vary.

Does everyone have a hand difference?

No. Some have only the chest-muscle difference and a functional hand. Others have short, small, missing or joined fingers or forearm differences. Individual examination determines the needs.

Is it inherited?

Most cases have no known affected relative, but rare familial cases occur and subtle signs can be missed. A genetics professional can review relatives and possible testing or other diagnoses. Do not assume one recurrence percentage applies to every family.

Can exercises or surgery cure every feature?

No. Individual therapy may improve movement and useful skills but cannot promise to create an absent muscle. Surgery can address selected goals, with risks, scars and possible revisions; perfect symmetry or normal strength is not guaranteed.

When is urgent help needed?

New pain, movement loss or breathing concerns need review. Severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips or skin, sudden confusion, or a child who becomes limp or unresponsive requires immediate emergency care. Follow specific postoperative instructions and do not dismiss new illness as part of the syndrome.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
